passage:
I'm Sangeeta, and I have lived across the landing from the Rao family for twelve years, so I've watched how it works in that flat. When the family shop slowed down, Siddharth's mother snapped at him for looking gloomy. When his sister's wedding budget grew, he was scolded for not helping enough. Everyone's worry seemed to land on him. His sister Meenal would look at her plate and say nothing.

Siddharth just smiles, takes the shopping bags and says, “I'll handle it.” I can't tell what he feels inside. Last week I found him sitting alone on the stairs for a long time. I asked if he wanted tea. “It's fine, Aunty,” he said. “They're just stressed.”

qa.q: How long has Sangeeta lived across the landing from the Rao family?
qa.a: Sangeeta has lived across the landing from the Rao family for twelve years.

qa.q: What does “They're just stressed” suggest about how Siddharth sees the situation?
qa.a: It suggests Siddharth excuses the family and swallows hurt to keep the peace, though the long time alone on the stairs hints at loneliness.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do next that respects the family's privacy but shows care?
qa.a: Sangeeta could keep offering tea and an ear, and gently say that Siddharth does not have to handle everything alone.

qa.q: What might Meenal be feeling when looking at the plate and saying nothing?
qa.a: Meenal may feel guilty and helpless, since the wedding budget is part of the pressure, and speaking up might turn the blame toward Meenal as well.

grounding: A person living across the landing observes a stressed family blaming one adult child for tensions that belong to the whole household.

passage:
First Sunday. The shop had lost a big order, and dinner was tight. Amma set a dish down hard. “Parul, why are you always so slow to help? There's no peace in this house because of you.” Parul stared at her rice. Her older sister Vasudha kept eating.

Two weeks later. Parul had stopped telling anyone about her day. She came home from work, went straight to her room and answered “fine” to every question. At dinner Papa sighed, and Amma glanced her way.

A month on. Vasudha found Parul on the terrace. “It isn't you,” she said. “Money is tight, everyone is scared, and you're the one who gets it.” Parul's eyes filled. “I thought I was the problem.” “Let's talk to Amma and Papa together,” said Vasudha.

qa.q: What did Amma say to Parul at the first Sunday dinner?
qa.a: Amma said, “Parul, why are you always so slow to help? There's no peace in this house because of you.”

qa.q: Why did Parul say, “I thought I was the problem”?
qa.a: Parul had been blamed at dinner and glanced at for weeks, and nobody had said the tension came from the money worries.

qa.q: What choice did Vasudha make on the terrace that shifted things?
qa.a: Vasudha told Parul it was not Parul's fault and suggested talking to Amma and Papa together.

qa.q: What might Vasudha have felt during the first dinner, eating quietly while Parul was blamed?
qa.a: Vasudha may have felt uneasy and afraid of being blamed next, which could explain the silence, and the talk on the terrace hints at guilt.

grounding: In a stressed family one member is blamed for tensions that belong to the whole household, and feels unseen until an older sister names it.

passage:
In the family's cloth shop in Barabanki, sales had been falling for two years. Abbu had loans he didn't discuss. Ammi had headaches. Asif's elder brother argued with everyone.
And somehow, every quarrel ended with Asif. “Since you went to Lucknow for that job, nothing has gone right.” “If you were here, the shop wouldn't be like this.” Even the burnt dal was, somehow, his fault for calling late.
Asif, twenty-four, sat on the shop's step on Sunday evening and stared at the road. Jahnavi from the medical store next door brought him tea. “They're scared,” she said. “It's easier to be angry at you than at the shop.”
Asif nodded. He hadn't thought of it like that. He'd only thought: I am the problem.

qa.q: Where was the family's cloth shop?
qa.a: It was in Barabanki.

qa.q: How was Asif feeling on the shop's step?
qa.a: He felt unseen and hurt, believing he was the problem, carrying the family's stress.

qa.q: What could help Asif with his family?
qa.a: He could gently name that the shop's troubles belong to everyone, perhaps with a calm family talk, instead of accepting all the blame.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi see the family's anger?
qa.a: She sees that the family is scared about the shop, and blaming Asif is easier than facing the real problem.

grounding: Shows a young man blamed by his stressed family for troubles that belong to the whole household, feeling unseen.

passage:
In the family's flat in Buenos Aires, Papa had been shouting more since losing his job. Mamá cried in the kitchen. Valentina's brother Tomás stayed out late.
And at dinner, it was always Valentina. “If you didn't argue with Papa, he wouldn't be so upset,” Mamá said. “You make everything worse,” said Tomás. Valentina had only asked if they could talk about money.
She moved out to share a flat with her friend Xin. But every Sunday lunch she felt it again, the family's eyes turning to her whenever the air got heavy.
Xin, driving her home one Sunday, asked, “Why do you always apologise to them?” Valentina looked out of the window. “Because someone has to be the reason. It's always been me.”

qa.q: Who does Valentina share a flat with?
qa.a: She shares a flat with her friend Xin.

qa.q: What does Valentina's answer to Xin suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels unseen and resigned, believing her role in the family is to carry the blame for tensions that aren't hers.

qa.q: What small step could help Valentina?
qa.a: She could stop apologising for things she didn't cause, and perhaps talk to a counsellor about the family pattern.

qa.q: How might Xin see the Sunday lunches?
qa.a: Xin seems puzzled and concerned, noticing Valentina keeps apologising for problems that belong to the whole family.

grounding: Shows a young woman blamed by her stressed family for tensions that belong to the whole household.

passage:
At the family counselling centre, the four of them sat in a row of plastic chairs. Mahima, the younger sister, spoke first. “Everything was fine until Shalini started this job with night shifts. Now Papa is angry, Mummy doesn't sleep.”
Papa nodded. Mummy looked at her hands.
Shalini said nothing. She had heard it so many times. When Papa's business partner cheated him, it was her fault for being out. When Mummy fell sick, it was her fault for not cooking.
The counsellor waited, then asked, “When did the stress in the house actually begin?” Papa hesitated. “Last year. With the business.”
Shalini looked up for the first time. The counsellor turned to her. “And how has it been for you, carrying it?”

qa.q: What did Mahima say started the trouble?
qa.a: She said everything was fine until Shalini started this job with night shifts.

qa.q: Why did Shalini say nothing at first?
qa.a: She felt unseen and tired, having heard the blame so many times that she no longer argued.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do that helped?
qa.a: The counsellor asked when the stress truly began, which showed it came from the business, and then asked how it felt for Shalini.

qa.q: How might Papa feel after admitting the stress began with the business?
qa.a: He may feel uncomfortable but also relieved to name the real source instead of blaming his daughter.

grounding: Shows a young woman blamed by her stressed family for tensions that began elsewhere, until a counsellor asks about the whole system.

passage:
Dear Harsha,
You asked on the phone why I didn't come home for Diwali. I've tried to say it for years, so here it is in writing.
Since Papa's shop closed, every argument at home somehow ends up being about me. Mummy and Papa fight about money, and then it's "Jahnavi's moods upset everyone." Dadi's knee gets worse, and it's because I "stress her with career talk." When you failed your Class 12 exam, Mummy said I'd distracted you with loud music. I was in Pune that year.
You're the good son, the quiet one. I don't blame you for that. But I think I've been carrying things that belong to all of us: the shop, the money, Papa's temper. It's easier to point at one person than to talk about those.
I'm not writing to fight. I just want one person at home to see it.
Your sister,
Jahnavi

qa.q: Where was Jahnavi when Harsha failed his Class 12 exam?
qa.a: Jahnavi was in Pune that year.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi feel about her place in the family?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels unseen and weighed down, tired of carrying blame for problems that belong to everyone.

qa.q: What is Jahnavi asking for, and why is it a sensible first step?
qa.a: Just for Harsha to see the pattern; one person at home noticing is a gentler start than a big family fight.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Harsha may feel surprised and uncomfortable, maybe a little guilty for never noticing how much blame landed on his sister.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a stressed family who is blamed for tensions that belong to the whole household and feels unseen.
